title: The lion in the well
hook: the hare shows the lion his own reflection in a well, and he leaps at it (Masnavi 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Masnavi's late hare walked slowly to the lion, and the lion's own hurry became his weakness.

Somewhere at work there's a person who drives you up the wall. Always interrupting. Always needing to be right. Always making it about themselves. And late one night, a small, unwelcome thought slips in: do I do that? It's tempting to slam the door on that thought. Rumi doesn't. The hare has arrived, very late, before a lion half mad with hunger. Why are you late? the lion roars. And the little hare, bowing, begins his story. Today, the lion in the well.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DRIVES YOU UP THE WALL.` → `DO I DO THAT?` → `THE LION IN THE WELL.`

segments.voice: Your majesty, I set out on time, with another hare as your meal. But on the road another lion stopped us. I told him we belong to the king of beasts. He laughed: who's your king? I'm the king here. He took my friend, and I barely got away to tell you. The lion is beside himself. Another lion, in my valley? Show me. So the hare leads him to a deep well. At the edge he hangs back and trembles. He's in there, the hare whispers, with my friend. The lion, in some tellings, tucks the hare under his arm for courage, and looks down. In the dark water a lion glares up at him, with a hare in its grip. He lets go of the real hare, roars, and leaps at the enemy. The water closes over him. The little hare runs home to the valley, and the animals rejoice. Then Rumi turns to us. The lion attacked his own face: he took his reflection for a rival and destroyed himself fighting it. So many of the faults you see in others, Rumi says, are your own nature looking back at you. You leap at the reflection and drown in your own anger. He points to a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: the believer is a mirror to the believer. What bothers you in someone else may be showing you yourself. That doesn't mean every fault you see is yours; sometimes the coworker really is rude. But before you leap, it's worth leaning over the well and asking: is that my face?
screen: `ANOTHER LION TOOK MY FRIEND.` · `THE HARE LEADS HIM TO A WELL.` · `HE LEAPS AT HIS OWN FACE.` · `WHAT YOU SEE MAY BE YOU.` · then, large: `THAT'S MY FACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who really bothers you, and name the exact thing: controlling, careless, loud, always late. Then gently lean over the well: is there a place in your life where you do some version of that too? You don't have to find one; if you do, don't scold yourself, just say inside, that's my face, and notice what happens to the anger.
Mirror. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad: the believer is a mirror to the believer, showing back what's really our own. Today's word.
Your line: that's my face. Sometimes the well is a mirror. That's day one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Masnavi often use the lion at the well to teach that the faults we see in others can reflect our own, pairing it with the saying that the believer is a mirror to the believer.

fork.setup: you're the lion, looking down the well. a lion glares up at you, holding a hare. what do you do?
options: look closer: is that my face?
walk away and let him keep the hare.
fork.reveal: the lion leaps and drowns. he fought his own reflection. Rumi's point is the second option: look before you leap.

original.note: Persian: a well. where the lion met his own face.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever hare tricks a dumb lion.
what it means: the strong one destroys himself fighting his own reflection.
what a scholar hears: Rumi reads the well as a mirror; he cites the saying al-mu'min mir'at al-mu'min, the believer is the believer's mirror (Abu Dawud 4918).
